```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 80)
has_data <- FSNA::fsna_data_available()
```

This vignette follows Porreca and Maturo (2026), the paper in which the exact
method is developed (manuscript submitted for publication, preprint forthcoming on arXiv; see `citation("FSNA")`). It
distinguishes the indices of Porreca, Maturo and Ventre (2025), computed by
applying the crisp formula to the three parameters of the TFNs and ranking
TFNs by their centre of gravity (`ijar_degree()`, `ijar_closeness()`,
`ijar_betweenness()`), from the fuzzy centrality defined by the extension
principle and computed exactly (`fuzzy_centrality()`).

The questionnaire data of the two departments analysed in the paper are not
distributed with the package (see `?fsna_questionnaire`). The examples use a
simulated network with the same structure: only half of the actors, the
respondents, send ties.

```{r}
library(FSNA)
A <- fsn_simulated(n = 40, respondents = 20, p = 0.25, seed = 1)
A
```

## The result

Read each TFN as a possibility distribution on the ill-known strength of a crisp
tie. The fuzzy centrality of actor $i$ defined by the extension principle is
$$\mu_{\tilde c_i}(v) = \sup\{\min_{kl}\mu_{kl}(W_{kl}) : c_i(W) = v\}.$$
If $c$ is continuous and non-decreasing in every tie on a box containing the
supports, its $\alpha$-cuts are
$$[\underline c_i(\alpha), \overline c_i(\alpha)] = [c_i(\underline W_\alpha), c_i(\overline W_\alpha)],$$
two crisp evaluations, on the lower and on the upper endpoints of the
$\alpha$-cuts of the ties. The class includes in- and out-strength, ordered
weighted averages of the ties, closeness based on any continuous t-norm and Katz
centrality. Betweenness and eigenvector centrality are excluded.

```{r}
idx <- c("in_strength", "in_closeness_min", "in_closeness_prod", "in_closeness_luk", "in_katz")
fcs <- lapply(idx, function(i) fuzzy_centrality(A, i))
names(fcs) <- idx
sapply(fcs, function(f) max(triangular_approx(f)$max_error))
```

The triangle $(c(L), c(M), c(R))$ is exact at the support and at the core; for
strength it is exact everywhere, for the nonlinear indices only at
$\alpha \in \{0, 1\}$ (dashed lines below).

```{r}
plot(fcs$in_closeness_min, actors = 5)
```

User-defined indices are accepted; `check_isotone()` tests monotonicity
numerically.

```{r}
my <- function(W) colSums(sqrt(W))
check_isotone(A, my, n_check = 20)
head(summary(fuzzy_centrality(A, my)), 3)
```

## Monte Carlo is an inner approximation

```{r}
mc <- mc_centrality(A, "in_closeness_prod", B = 200)
f <- fcs$in_closeness_prod
summary((mc$upper - mc$lower) / (f$upper[, 1] - f$lower[, 1]))
```

## Comparing actors

`possibility_matrix()` returns $\Pi(i \succeq j)$ and $N(i \succ j)$. They are
exact for in- and out-strength and for ordered weighted averages of the
incoming or outgoing ties, whose values for two actors depend on disjoint ties,
and bounds otherwise. The supremum lies between two levels of the grid: it is
found by linear interpolation for strength, which is exact, and by bisection on
$\alpha$ for the other indices, computing the exact cuts at each trial level
(Algorithm 1 of Porreca and Maturo, 2026; tolerance $10^{-4}$). Taking it as
the largest grid level at which the condition holds overestimates necessity.

```{r}
fp <- fcs$in_closeness_prod
P_bis <- possibility_matrix(fp)$possibility             # bisection (default)
P_grid <- possibility_matrix(fp, "grid")$possibility    # largest grid level
off <- row(P_bis) != col(P_bis)
summary(P_bis[off] - P_grid[off])                        # at most one grid step
```

```{r}
cmp <- possibility_matrix(fcs$in_strength)
cmp
plot(cmp)
certification(fcs$in_strength)
```

An ordering is *certified* when the supports are strictly separated: then it
holds in every compatible network. A necessity equal to one does not imply this.

```{r}
C0 <- certified_pairs(fcs$in_strength, 0)
sum(C0) / choose(nrow(C0), 2)
```

The fuzzy set of the most central actor and the possible ranks:

```{r}
sort(top_set(fcs$in_strength), decreasing = TRUE)[1:6]
head(rank_intervals(fcs$in_strength, 0.5), 6)
plot(fcs$in_strength, type = "intervals")
```

## Null or unknown ties

By default a pair without a rating is a null tie. `set_unknown()` treats the
ties that non-respondents would have sent as unknown: vacuous possibility
distributions on $[0, 1]$, whose cuts are the whole interval at every level.
The exact methods propagate this ignorance.

```{r}
Au <- set_unknown(A, "nonrespondents")
Au
certification(fuzzy_centrality(Au, "in_strength"))$proportion_certified
length(top_set(fuzzy_centrality(Au, "in_strength"), alpha = 0.5))
```

When the non-respondents could have sent ties of any strength, few orderings
survive: the rankings depend on the convention that unrated pairs are null
ties.

## Ranking methods

Nine methods are available: five scores (centre of gravity, core, Yager's index,
graded mean or possibilistic mean, Liou-Wang total integral value) and four
methods based on the comparisons (net possibility, necessity dominance,
certified dominance, membership in the top set).

```{r}
cr <- compare_rankings(fcs$in_closeness_prod,
                       c("cog", "core", "yager", "graded_mean", "liou_wang", "possibility", "necessity", "certified", "top"))
round(cr$correlation, 2)
```

## Simulation study

`simulation_study()` evaluates coverage of latent centralities, Monte Carlo
approximations, the error of the triangle and the reliability of certified
orderings on networks simulated with `simulate_fsn()`. A small run:

```{r}
sim <- simulation_study(n = 20, p = 0.3, kappa = c(1, 3), nrep = 3,
                        indices = c("in_strength", "in_closeness_prod"), B = 50)
summary(sim)[, c("index", "kappa", "coverage_exact", "coverage_mc50", "disc_cog",
                 "disc_cog_uncertified", "cert0", "wrong_among_cert0")]
```


## Reproduction of Table 4 of Porreca and Maturo (2026)

The following code reproduces Table 4 of the paper. It needs the questionnaire
data (`?fsna_questionnaire`) and is not run when they are not available. With
the default arguments `fsn_department()` builds the networks analysed in the
paper: ratings mapped to $[0, 1]$ by $x \mapsto (x-1)/4$, so that the answer
Never is the absence of a tie, unrated pairs and ratings with incomplete
trajectories as null ties, later ratings replacing earlier ones, and actors
without ties excluded (51 actors with 24 respondents and 55 actors with 28
respondents).

```{r, eval = has_data}
DA <- fsn_department("A"); DB <- fsn_department("B")
tab4 <- function(x, ix) {
  fc <- fuzzy_centrality(x, ix); n <- n_actors(x); np <- n * (n - 1) / 2
  core <- fc$lower[, ncol(fc$lower)]
  c(cert0 = sum(certified_pairs(fc, 0)) / np, cert05 = sum(certified_pairs(fc, 0.5)) / np,
    alg1 = certification(fc)$N1_not_separated, grid = certification(fc)$N1_not_separated_grid,
    spearman = cor(fc_score(fc, "cog", triangle = TRUE), core, method = "spearman"),
    top05 = length(top_set(fc, alpha = 0.5)), top1 = length(top_set(fc, alpha = 1)),
    width = mean(fc$upper[, 1] - fc$lower[, 1]))
}
ix4 <- c("in_strength", "in_closeness_min", "in_closeness_prod", "in_katz")
round(t(sapply(ix4, function(i) tab4(DA, i))), 3)
round(t(sapply(ix4, function(i) tab4(DB, i))), 3)
```
